faq.a: Insulin, through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, promotes glycogenesis, lipogenesis and protein synthesis.
faq.q: What hormone is the main driver of anabolism?

faq.a: Cytokines inhibit mTOR and increase proteolysis, leading to muscle wasting and impaired wound healing.
They are rarely available; focus on nutrition and insulin therapy instead, as steroids carry bleeding and infection risks.
faq.q: Can we use anabolic steroids in low‑resource settings?

exam: A 45‑year‑old diabetic patient presents with weight loss and muscle wasting. What is the most likely underlying mechanism? — Insulin resistance leading to impaired mTOR activation and decreased protein synthesis.
A child with severe malaria shows hypoglycemia after fasting. What metabolic pathway is most affected? — Glycogenesis is suppressed due to low insulin and high glucagon.
During a ward round you note a patient with high CRP and low albumin. What does this suggest about his anabolic state? — Chronic inflammation is inhibiting anabolism, leading to hypoalbuminemia.
A patient with chronic kidney disease has low serum albumin but normal protein intake. What is the likely cause? — Reduced hepatic synthesis due to uremic toxins and inflammation.
You are treating a patient with septic shock. Which drug should be avoided because it suppresses mTOR? — Corticosteroids (high doses) suppress mTOR and worsen catabolism.
A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy develops muscle wasting. What adjunct therapy could help? — Nutritional support with adequate protein and possibly anabolic agents if available.
You observe a patient with fatty liver on ultrasound. What metabolic imbalance is responsible? — Excessive lipogenesis due to insulin resistance and overnutrition.
A patient with severe burns shows delayed wound healing. What metabolic process is impaired? — Protein synthesis via mTOR is suppressed by inflammatory cytokines.
ai.title: Anabolism in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Anabolism is the energy‑using synthesis of macromolecules, driven mainly by insulin and growth hormone. Clinically it underpins muscle gain, fat storage and recovery from catabolic states such as infection or trauma.

b: Glycogenesis – glucose to glycogen
Lipogenesis – fatty acids to triglycerides
Protein synthesis – amino acids to polypeptides
sections.p: Anabolism refers to the constructive metabolic pathways that build complex molecules from simpler precursors, consuming ATP. In the body it is essential for growth, repair and energy storage.

b: Insulin binds IGF‑1 receptor → PI3K/AKT → mTOR activation
mTOR stimulates ribosomal biogenesis and translation
Insulin also activates glycogen synthase and fatty acid synthase
sections.p: Hormones such as insulin, growth hormone and IGF‑1 activate intracellular pathways (PI3K/AKT, mTOR) that increase enzyme activity for biosynthesis and reduce catabolic enzymes.

b: High ATP → inhibits glycogen phosphorylase
Low glucose → activates glucagon, suppressing glycogenesis
Amino acid levels regulate mTOR via Rag GTPases
sections.p: Anabolism is tightly regulated by energy status, hormonal milieu and nutrient availability. Negative feedback from ATP, glucose and amino acids modulates enzyme activity.

b: Diabetes mellitus – insulin resistance reduces anabolism
Sepsis – cytokines inhibit mTOR, causing cachexia
Malnutrition – amino acid deficiency limits protein synthesis
sections.p: Impaired anabolism leads to muscle wasting, hypoglycemia, and poor wound healing. Excessive anabolism can cause fatty liver, obesity and insulin resistance.
Recognising anabolic deficits guides nutritional support, insulin therapy and anabolic agents. In low‑resource settings, simple bedside tests and clinical signs are vital.

t.b: Low albumin suggests protein anabolism failure; indicates malnutrition or chronic inflammation.
High CRP indicates inflammation that suppresses anabolism; guides need for anti‑inflammatory therapy.
Hypoglycemia in fasting patients may reflect impaired glycogenesis; treat with dextrose and insulin adjustment.

b: Protein‑rich diet (1.2–1.5 g/kg/day)
Insulin therapy in diabetes to promote glycogenesis
Recombinant human growth hormone in severe catabolic states (if available)
sections.p: Treat underlying cause, provide adequate protein and calories, use insulin or anabolic steroids cautiously, monitor for complications.

b: Anabolism vs Catabolism
Cachexia vs Sarcopenia
sections.p: Catabolism is the opposite process, breaking down molecules for energy. Cachexia involves both increased catabolism and reduced anabolism.

b: Albumin <35 g/L may be due to fluid overload
sections.p: Low serum albumin can be due to dilution or liver disease, not only malnutrition. Normal glucose may mask impaired glycogenesis in early sepsis.

b: Insulin ↑ → glycogenesis, lipogenesis, protein synthesis
sections.p: In exam questions, look for clues about hormonal status, nutritional state and inflammatory markers. Remember that insulin promotes anabolism; glucagon does the opposite.

b: Severe hypoglycemia (blood glucose <2.5 mmol/L)
sections.p: Urgent care needed for hypoglycemia, severe muscle wasting, or signs of organ failure due to metabolic derangement.
